items.gist: Introduces the aṇu procedure for attaining the supreme state. It distinguishes vikalpa, niścaya, and the levels of buddhi, prāṇa, body, and knower.
Describes anuttara meditation on the heart cakra and its twelve goddesses. The yogi dissolves the universe into consciousness through this practice.
Explains prāṇa functions as an upāya for revealing the supreme. It maps prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna to stages of bliss.
Presents visarga as the divine emission and source of bliss. The practitioner rests in the heart through its nāḍī and cakra processes.
Details uccāra practice and the flow of visarga amṛta. It connects mantra, nāḍīs, and the dissolution of the six paths.
Describes the subtle liṅga of Śiva-Śakti and its threefold manifestation. It emphasizes resting in the liṅga and pūjā.
Explains karaṇa as a sevenfold practice preceded by knowledge. It prepares the transition to the supreme state.
Treats varṇa as seed-sound and mantra as consciousness-revealing. Repetition and contemplation lead to cidātmatā.
Contrasts external and internal methods of practice. It stresses gradual cultivation for less advanced practitioners.
Lists five signs: bliss, trembling, sleep, and whirling. These mark entry into cakra sovereignty.
Relates kuṇḍalī, visarga, and the heart liṅga. It describes the yogi's absorption in Śiva-Śakti.
Explains bīja and mantra as consciousness-spanda. It emphasizes their role in revealing the supreme.
Gives the uccāra procedure and its subtle correspondences. It culminates in non-dual consciousness.
Describes varṇa japa and visualization of bindu and fire. The practitioner attains identity with Śiva.
Orders the methods from aṇu to anuttara. It concludes that the external aṇu path is clearly taught.
Closes ahnika five with the aṇu upāya summary. It affirms the path to the supreme state.
